questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The core claim of a formalist reading
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a formalist claim asserts about a text.
questions.stem: A formalist claim is stated in a single sentence, and the log asks what that sentence asserts.

options.text: That the text mirrors the world outside it, so its images can be checked against events
options.misconception: treats a formal reading as a claim about the world

options.text: That the text is a record of its author's private state, so feeling is the real subject
options.misconception: reads the formal claim as a claim about the author's mind

options.text: That the text's own arrangement is what produces its meaning, and that meaning is made in the text
That the text belongs to a tradition, so its devices matter only as inherited borrowing
options.misconception: reduces the formal claim to a claim about inheritance

questions.explanation: The core claim of a formalist reading is that meaning is produced by the text's own arrangement of language. A claim about the world, about the author's feelings, or about inherited borrowing each introduces something the reading does not need.
questions.hint: Look for the text doing the work.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A claim about language beside a claim about moment
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a claim about language from a claim about a moment.

stimulus.body: Entry for 18 June: I have two readings pinned above the tank. One says the poem repeats a word three times in the last stanza and builds the pressure there. The other says the poem was written in the winter of the fever and the same word means something different in a house with a sick child. They are about the same poem and they do not say the same kind of thing.

questions.stem: Two readings sit side by side, one about a repeated word and one about a historical moment.

options.text: The first is a claim about language and the second a claim about the moment of writing
Both are claims about the moment, since repetition is itself a historical practice
options.misconception: absorbs every technical observation into historical explanation

options.text: Both are claims about language, since a poem's words are fixed and a date is only a detail
options.misconception: reduces historical questions to matters of wording

options.text: Neither is a claim at all, since a reader may only describe what is plainly on the page
options.misconception: believes description is the only permitted kind of reading

questions.explanation: The first reading concerns how the poem's language is arranged, the second concerns the conditions of its making, and the two answer different questions. Folding technique into history or history into wording, and refusing to make claims at all, each erases the distinction.
questions.hint: Ask what each reading is about.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a formal reading counts
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a formal reading counts as evidence.
questions.stem: The tank notes explain what a formal reading actually counts as evidence.

answer.exemplar: A formal reading counts what is present in the text and organised: repetitions, placements, lengths, sound patterns, the order in which things are said, and the terms the poem refuses. What it counts is evidence about the making of meaning rather than about the world or the writer, so a feature only becomes evidence once a reader shows what work it does in that particular arrangement. A count on its own settles nothing, because any text can be tallied in many ways, and the tally means only what the argument makes of it.

questions.explanation: A formal reading counts features of arrangement, and each becomes evidence only when a reader shows the work it does in that arrangement. A bare count settles nothing, since the tally means whatever the argument makes of it.
questions.hint: A count needs an argument to mean anything.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A formal reading asked to connect a device to a subject
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the difficulty of linking a device to a subject formally.
questions.stem: A formal reading is asked to connect a device to a subject, and the log shows the difficulty.

options.text: The link is automatic, since a device always points at the theme the poem is about
options.misconception: assumes a device points at only one theme by itself

options.text: The link is impossible, since a subject cannot be established from arrangement at all
options.misconception: believes subject matter can never be reached by formal means

options.text: The link must be shown, since the same device can carry different subjects in different texts
The link is unnecessary, since a reading of the arrangement is already a reading of the subject
options.misconception: assumes arrangement alone settles what a text is about

questions.explanation: The link must be shown, because the same device carries different subjects in different texts and only the arrangement can establish which is at work. Assuming an automatic link, refusing the link altogether, and treating arrangement as already a subject all dodge the demonstration.
questions.hint: Show the work the device does here.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Looking for the system beneath a text
questions.learningObjective: Explain what would count as finding a system beneath a text.
questions.stem: A reader looks for the system beneath a text and the log asks what will count as finding it.

options.text: Finding a pattern that was not visible before, which shows the reader's attention has been repaid
options.misconception: treats any newly noticed pattern as a discovered system

options.text: Finding a rule set that predicts what the text does in cases the reader has not yet read
options.misconception: accepts a rule that only covers what has already been read

options.text: Finding an arrangement that explains several features at once without needing separate exceptions
options.misconception: prefers a rule with many exceptions over a simpler one

options.text: Finding a rule set that the text obeys in cases not yet read, and that other texts do not obey

questions.explanation: A system is found when it predicts untried cases and distinguishes this text from others, since a rule that covers only what has been read is a description. Novelty, simplicity, and unexplained exceptions each mistake a finding for a system.
questions.hint: A rule should reach cases you have not read.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A convention mistaken for a statement
questions.learningObjective: Identify the difference between a convention and a statement.
questions.stem: A convention is mistaken for a statement, and the log asks what the difference is.

options.text: A convention is shared practice, while a statement is what a particular writer asserts here
A convention is old and a statement is new, so age is the only difference between them
options.misconception: reduces the difference to the age of the practice

options.text: A convention is written down and a statement is spoken, so the medium tells them apart
options.misconception: believes the medium alone distinguishes convention from statement

options.text: A convention is what many readers accept, while a statement is what no reader accepts
options.misconception: defines a statement by the absence of agreement

questions.explanation: A convention is shared practice that many texts follow, while a statement is what this writer asserts in this place, and the confusion between them is what makes a text seem to say more than it does. Age, medium, and reader agreement each misdescribe the distinction.
questions.hint: Shared practice or a particular assertion?

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a historical reading restores
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a historical reading restores to a text.

stimulus.body: Entry for 9 September: the reading was supposed to be formal, all arrangement and repetition, and it worked, until somebody asked what the letter's mention of a third son meant. The poet had lost two children. The repetition of 'third' is not a figure for anything; it is a fact about a house where two were buried. I am not sure the formal reading is wrong, but it is incomplete now.

questions.stem: A historical reading is offered where a formal one was expected, and the log asks what it restores.

options.text: It restores nothing, since the arrangement alone accounted for every effect in the poem
options.misconception: claims a formal reading already accounts for everything

options.text: It restores the circumstances the arrangement was made in, which changes what the features are
It restores the author's intention, since only the writer knows what the words were for
options.misconception: treats historical context as a route to certain intention

options.text: It restores a better version, since a poem set in its own time is always clearer
options.misconception: assumes historical setting makes a text easier to read

questions.explanation: A historical reading restores the circumstances in which the arrangement was made, which changes what the features turn out to be. Total sufficiency, certain intention, and the assumption that context simplifies a text each misdescribe what the restoration does.
questions.hint: What were the circumstances of the arrangement?

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The core claim of a formalist reading
questions.learningObjective: State the core claim a formalist reading makes about meaning.
questions.stem: An entry of 14 May states the core claim that a formalist reading makes about a text.

answer.exemplar: A formalist reading claims that the text's meaning is made in the text, by the arrangement of its parts, and that this arrangement can be described exactly enough for another reader to check the description. The claim is not that the world or the writer is irrelevant, but that the meaning a reader receives is the meaning the arrangement produces. That is why the reading can say what a passage does without asking what the author believed or what was happening outside the book.

questions.explanation: The core claim is that meaning is produced by the arrangement of the text's parts, in terms another reader could check. It does not deny the world or the writer, but it locates meaning in what the arrangement does rather than in what lies behind it.
questions.hint: Meaning is made in the arrangement.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A claim about language beside a claim about moment
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a claim about language from a claim about a moment.
questions.stem: A claim about language and a claim about the moment of writing are set against each other.

options.text: The language claim describes how the text works, the moment claim describes when and where it was made
The language claim is stronger, since arrangement survives every change of circumstance
options.misconception: assumes one kind of claim always outranks the other

options.text: They are the same claim, since a poem's language is a product of the moment that made it
options.misconception: collapses technique and historical moment into one thing

options.text: Neither can be checked, since language is subjective and dates are commonly wrong
options.misconception: denies that either kind of claim can be tested

questions.explanation: A claim about language describes how the text works, while a claim about a moment describes when and where it was made, and the two are answered by different evidence. Ranking them, collapsing them, and calling both unchecked each refuse the distinction that makes them usable.
questions.hint: How it works is not when it was made.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a formal reading counts
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate what a count of features establishes.
questions.stem: A formalist reader counts five features of a poem, and the log asks what the count establishes.

options.text: That the poem is well made, since five deliberate features cannot be accidental
options.misconception: treats the number of features as proof of quality

options.text: That a pattern exists, though the count alone leaves the pattern's meaning open
That the poem means what the count suggests, since the features are the poem's content
options.misconception: equates a description of features with a reading of meaning

options.text: That the features were planned, since no writer repeats a word by chance in a short poem
options.misconception: treats repetition as proof of intention

questions.explanation: A count of features establishes that a pattern is there to be examined, while the pattern's meaning stays open until a reader shows the work it does. Quality, completed meaning, and proof of planning each claim more from a tally than a tally can carry.
questions.hint: The count shows there is a pattern, not its sense.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A formal reading asked to connect a device to a subject
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a device to subject link must show.
questions.stem: A device is linked to a subject in a formal reading, and the log asks what the link must show.

options.text: That the device is rare in the period, since a rare device cannot be carrying a common subject
options.misconception: judges a device by its frequency in the period

options.text: That the text would work differently without the device, since the subject depends on the arrangement
That the author intended the subject, since devices do not appear by accident in finished work
options.misconception: infers intention from the presence of a device

options.text: That the device belongs to the subject's tradition, since inherited forms carry their meanings forward
options.misconception: grounds the link in inherited practice rather than in the text

questions.explanation: The link is shown when the text would work differently without the device, since that is what ties the arrangement to the subject. Rarity, intention, and inherited practice are all claims about the device's history rather than its work in this text.
questions.hint: Take the device away and see what changes.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Looking for the system beneath a text
questions.learningObjective: Identify how a reader mistakes an imposed rule for a found system.
questions.stem: A reader hunts for the system beneath a text and the log warns against a false one.

options.text: A system that explains every poem in the set with one rule and no exceptions at all
options.misconception: treats the absence of exceptions as proof of a true system

options.text: A system fitted to the poems after the fact, so each poem is read to fit the rule
A system that the writer is said to have followed, since a named habit is a real system
options.misconception: accepts a writer's claimed habit as a discovered structure

options.text: A system drawn from the period's rules, since old forms always underlie later arrangements
options.misconception: assumes a period's forms underlie any text's arrangement

questions.explanation: A false system is one fitted to the poems after the fact, so each poem is bent to fit the rule rather than the rule found in the poems. Flawless coverage, a named habit, and inherited forms each mistake a hypothesis for a discovered structure.
questions.hint: Did the rule find the poems or the poems fit it?

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A convention mistaken for a statement
questions.learningObjective: Analyse how a convention is read as a personal confession.

stimulus.body: Entry for 27 July: the poem closes with the stock figure of the empty chair and the unswept hearth, which every elegy of the period ends with. The student in the reading group has written that the poet is confessing that he cannot let go of his sister. I said nothing for a while. The stanza is the shape elegies take, and the poet has filled it in ways that are his own, but the form is doing half the saying.

questions.stem: A convention of elegy is read as a personal confession, and the tank note asks about it.

options.text: The student is right, since a convention carries the same feeling in every poem that uses it
options.misconception: believes a convention fixes the feeling a poem expresses

options.text: The student is right, since no writer would use a shape unless it suited what he felt
options.misconception: infers personal feeling from a writer's choice of form

options.text: The student is right, since elegies were written for readers who knew the conventions
options.misconception: grounds a personal reading in the audience's knowledge

options.text: The convention supplies the shape, so the confession is the writer's addition to a shared form

questions.explanation: The convention supplies the shape of the closing and the writer adds the particular feeling, so a shared form cannot by itself carry a confession. Uniform feeling, suitability as proof of feeling, and reader knowledge each confuse the given with the added.
questions.hint: What is given, and what is added?

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a historical reading restores
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a historical reading restores to a text.
questions.stem: A note of 3 June explains what a historical reading restores to a text.

answer.exemplar: A historical reading restores the circumstances that made a text's devices legible: the events the poem was written against, the situations of its first readers, the rules of the occasion it obeyed, and the physical conditions of its making. Without that setting a reader sees a word and hears a mystery; with it, the word is an ordinary usage and the mystery has a shape. The restoration does not replace a formal reading but supplies the conditions under which the arrangement does its work, and it can also show that what looked like a device was simply what the moment required.

questions.explanation: A historical reading restores the circumstances that made devices legible, supplying the conditions under which the arrangement works. It does not replace a formal reading, and it can show that an apparent device was simply what the moment required.
questions.hint: Restore the conditions of the arrangement.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The core claim of a formalist reading
questions.learningObjective: Correct a formalist claim that has been stated too widely.
questions.stem: A reader states a formal claim in the wrong terms and the log asks for a correction.

options.text: The poem's imagery proves that the writer believed what the poem says about the world
options.misconception: treats imagery as evidence for a writer's belief

options.text: The poem's imagery proves that the period shared what the poem says about the world
options.misconception: reads the poem's images as evidence for a period's beliefs

options.text: The poem's imagery makes the poem mean what it says about the world, whatever the writer believed
The poem's imagery is decorative, since arrangement cannot carry meaning on its own
options.misconception: denies that arrangement can carry meaning

questions.explanation: The corrected claim is that a poem's arrangement makes it mean what it says, whatever the writer believed or the period shared. The other three versions smuggle a belief into the reading or strip the reading of meaning altogether.
questions.hint: Keep the claim about the text itself.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A claim about language beside a claim about moment
questions.learningObjective: Compare a formal claim and a claim about a text's moment.
questions.stem: Two claims about the same poem are compared, one formal and one about its moment.

options.text: That each answers a different question, so the poem needs both readings rather than a choice between them
That the formal claim is the true one, since the moment only adds noise to the arrangement
options.misconception: dismisses historical explanation as noise beside analysis

options.text: That the claim about the moment is the true one, since context explains everything a formal reading notes
options.misconception: makes context a total explanation of textual features

options.text: That the two claims cancel each other out, since a text can only be read one way at a time
options.misconception: treats two readings as mutually exclusive

questions.explanation: A formal claim and a claim about a text's moment answer different questions, so the poem needs both rather than a choice between them. Ranking one as true, making context a total explanation, and treating the readings as rivals each misdescribe their relation.
questions.hint: They ask different questions of the poem.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a formal reading counts
questions.learningObjective: Explain why counting features is not the same as describing a text.
questions.stem: The log explains why counting features is not the same as describing a text.

answer.exemplar: Counting records that something is there, three times, in a particular position, and it can be done by anyone with the text in front of them. Describing says what the thing does, which is why the same number can support different readings depending on the argument: three repetitions may gather a stanza towards a close or interrupt a rhythm to keep a reader uneasy. The count is the fixed part of the evidence, and the description is the part a reader has to argue for and another reader can dispute.

questions.explanation: Counting records what is there, while describing says what it does, and the same count can support different readings. The tally is the fixed evidence; the description is the part that must be argued and can be disputed.
questions.hint: The count is fixed; the work is argued.

questions.topic: A formal reading asked to connect a device to a subject
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate whether a formal link between device and subject holds.
questions.stem: A formal reading links a repeated phrase to a theme and the entry asks whether the link holds.

options.text: It holds, since a repeated phrase is by definition the poem's most important idea
options.misconception: treats frequency as proof of thematic importance

options.text: It holds, since the phrase appears at the ends of lines, which is where important things go
options.misconception: assumes line-ending placement marks importance by itself

options.text: It holds, since the theme of the poem is fixed in advance by its title page
options.misconception: takes the title as a statement of what the poem must be about

options.text: It holds only if the phrase's positions are shown to shape the theme, not merely to repeat it

questions.explanation: The link holds only when the phrase's positions are shown to shape the theme, since a repetition that does no work cannot carry it. Frequency, line-ending placement, and the title page each assert the connection rather than demonstrate it.
questions.hint: Repetition is not yet a link.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Looking for the system beneath a text
questions.learningObjective: Apply the test of a system to a proposed rule.

stimulus.body: Entry for 5 January: the student says every poem in the little green book turns on a loss of something named by a colour, and she has the pages to prove it. I ask her what the next poem in the sequence does. She cannot answer, and then she finds a blue jar that does not appear until page forty. She adjusts the rule and the poem fits. At that point I am no longer sure what the rule is for.

questions.stem: A reader proposes a system of three rules for a set of poems and the log tests it.

options.text: The system is sound, since three clear rules are better evidence than one
options.misconception: judges a system by the number of its rules

options.text: The system is sound, since the poems on the page do fit the rules as stated
options.misconception: accepts fit on the examined pages as proof of a system

options.text: The system is unsound, since adjusting it to fit each poem means the poems are not testing it
The system cannot be judged, since no reader could ever read enough poems to be certain
options.misconception: treats a system as requiring exhaustive verification

questions.explanation: A rule that is adjusted whenever a poem resists is not being tested by those poems, so the set of poems has stopped being evidence. Number of rules, fit on the examined pages, and the impossibility of certainty each avoid the real defect in the proposal.
questions.hint: Ask whether the poems could refute it.

questions.topic: A convention mistaken for a statement
questions.learningObjective: Identify why a conventional ending is not the writer's conviction.
questions.stem: A conventional ending is treated as the author's own conviction, and the log objects.

options.text: Because the convention was available to every writer, so any writer could have chosen it deliberately
options.misconception: argues that availability makes a convention meaningless

options.text: Because the convention carries the expectation it was built to carry, and the writer adds to it
Because the ending is short, and short endings are always borrowed rather than chosen
options.misconception: judges a convention by the length of the passage using it

options.text: Because readers prefer conventional endings, so the writer wrote it to please the crowd
options.misconception: explains a convention by the audience's preferences

questions.explanation: A conventional ending carries the expectation it was built to carry, and what the writer adds to that shape is the part that is the writer's own. Availability, length, and audience preference each mistake a shared practice for a personal conviction.
questions.hint: The shape is shared; the filling is the writer's.

questions.topic: What a historical reading restores
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a formal and a historical reading each leave out.
questions.stem: A historical reading is set beside a formal one and the log asks what each leaves out.

options.text: The formal reading leaves out the conditions of the text, the historical one leaves out the text's arrangement
Both leave out the author, since no reading can reach the person who wrote the poem
options.misconception: treats the writer as permanently out of reach of both readings

options.text: Neither leaves anything out, since together they cover every ground a reader could want
options.misconception: assumes two readings between them account for everything

options.text: The historical reading leaves out the text, since context matters more than wording
options.misconception: prizes context above the words of the poem

questions.explanation: A formal reading leaves out the conditions of the text and a historical reading leaves out the arrangement itself, which is why each is needed alongside the other. The author's absence, total coverage, and the priority of context each misdescribe the two readings.
questions.hint: Each reading has its own blind spot.

questions.topic: The core claim of a formalist reading
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate how to narrow an overbroad formal claim.
questions.stem: A formalist claim is stated too broadly and the entry asks how to narrow it.

options.text: By adding a second claim about the period, since two claims together are harder to refute
options.misconception: believes a wider claim is safer when backed by another claim

options.text: By attaching it to a particular text, since the claim was never true of any text at large
options.misconception: asserts the broad claim was simply false everywhere

options.text: By stating which features and which arrangement it concerns, so another reader can test it
By weakening the words until nothing could contradict it, since a claim that cannot fail is safe
options.misconception: prefers unfalsifiable claims for their safety

questions.explanation: An overbroad claim is narrowed by stating which features and which arrangement it concerns, so that another reader can test it against the text. Padding it with a second claim, insisting it was never true at all, and softening it into unfalsifiability each avoid the work of testing.
questions.hint: Specify what the claim is about.

options.text: The reading about rhythm is the formal one, since it describes how the poem's language is arranged

options.text: Neither is a reading, since one describes sound and the other describes dates
options.misconception: denies that either sort of remark can be a reading

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a formal reading counts
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a formal reading counts and what it passes over.
questions.stem: The tank notes describe what a formal reading counts and what it passes over.

answer.exemplar: A formal reading counts repetitions, positions, lengths, sound relations, syntactic turns, and the order in which the poem lays out its parts. What it passes over is everything the text does not arrange: what the moment supplied, what a reader in the author's situation would have brought to the words, and the occasions of publication that shaped what a reader expected. That second list is not a criticism of the method but the boundary of it, and a reading that stays inside the count can say precisely what it knows and no more.

questions.explanation: A formal reading counts repetitions, positions, lengths, and sound relations, while passing over what the moment supplied and what readers brought. That boundary is not a defect but the limit of what the count can know.
questions.hint: Know the boundary of the count.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A formal reading asked to connect a device to a subject
questions.learningObjective: Apply what a formal link between device and subject must show.

stimulus.body: Entry for 2 October: the sonnet turns at the ninth line and the student says the turn proves the poem changes its moral mind, so the closing lines must be read as the poet's settled opinion. I asked her what the ninth line actually does to the argument. She said it changes the time the speaker is talking about. So we have a turn, and we have a shift in tense, and neither of those is yet a change of mind.

questions.stem: A sonnet's volta is claimed to prove a moral turn, and the entry asks what would show it.

options.text: The claim stands, since a turn in a sonnet is by definition a change of belief
options.misconception: takes the technical term to settle what kind of turn occurred

options.text: The claim stands, since the closing lines are the part a reader remembers and therefore believes
options.misconception: confuses memorable placement with conviction

options.text: The claim stands, since sonnets of the period were written to argue a settled case

questions.topic: A convention mistaken for a statement
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a convention comes to be read as a statement.

answer.exemplar: A convention becomes a statement when the context that explained it goes missing, because a convention only means what its use explains. An elegy closes with the empty chair because elegies close that way, and when the practice is forgotten the chair is left standing as evidence of a private grief the writer never claimed. The reading that treats a shape as an assertion is usually a reading that has lost the setting, and recovering the setting restores the difference between what the form says and what the writer says.

questions.explanation: A convention becomes a statement when the context that explained it goes missing, since a convention only means what its use explains. A reading that finds private grief in a shared shape has usually lost the setting that explained it.

answer.exemplar: A system is found rather than imposed when the reader begins from features that resist explanation and lets the pattern emerge from them, and then tests the pattern on texts where it was not hoped for. questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a formal reading counts
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a formal reading counts features as its evidence.
questions.stem: The log explains why a formal reading counts features as its evidence.

answer.exemplar: A formal reading counts features because the features are the only part of a text that a reader can point to twice and get the same answer. Another reader holding the same poem will find the same repetitions, the same line lengths, and the same turns of syntax, so an argument built on them can be checked rather than merely believed. That is why the count comes first in the method and why a description of what a feature does comes second: the fixed part is what makes the disputable part arguable, and without it a reading floats free of the page.

questions.explanation: Features are counted because another reader will find the same ones, which makes an argument built on them checkable. The count comes first because the fixed part is what makes the disputable description of its work arguable.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A convention mistaken for a statement
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a convention cannot be quoted as a belief.
questions.stem: A note explains why a convention cannot be quoted as an author's belief.

answer.exemplar: A convention cannot be quoted as a belief because quoting it means the words were chosen freely for what they say, and a convention is chosen for what it does. The turn of a line that every elegy of the period turns on says nothing about the poet's grief any more than the words of a set form in a sonnet say what the writer thought on the day. What a writer believes may be inferable from how the convention is filled, but the convention itself is the shape shared with everyone else who wrote in the form at the time.

questions.explanation: Quoting a convention as a belief treats shared practice as free choice, and what a writer believes can only be inferred from how the convention is filled. The convention is the shape shared with everyone else writing in the form at the time.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The core claim of a formalist reading
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a formal claim concerns the text and not the world.

answer.exemplar: A formal claim is a claim about the text because the only evidence it uses is the text's own arrangement, and any claim about the world would need evidence from outside it. Saying that a poem's images show what the writer believed, or what the period believed, or what is true of the world, each asks the reader to believe something the arrangement alone cannot establish. The formal claim is narrower and more checkable, because it says what the poem does with its language and stops there, and the world is allowed to be a separate question.

questions.explanation: A formal claim uses only the text's arrangement as evidence, so it cannot support a claim about the world without outside evidence. Its narrowness is what makes it checkable, and the world remains a separate question.

questions.topic: What a historical reading restores

answer.exemplar: A historical reading restores the expectations a text was written to meet, and those expectations are what made a device legible in the first place. options.text: That the arrangement belongs to a school of writing that produced it
options.misconception: treats arrangement as the mark of a literary school

options.text: That the arrangement is what distinguishes this poem from the ones written before it
options.misconception: makes a comparative claim from a formal description

questions.explanation: The claim is that the arrangement makes the poem mean what it means, in terms another reader could check against the page. A symptom of the writer's mind, a marker of a school, and a claim of originality each go beyond what arrangement alone asserts.
questions.hint: Meaning made, and checkable.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A claim about language beside a claim about moment
questions.learningObjective: Identify what kind of claim each reading makes.

stimulus.body: Entry for 4 November: the two paragraphs I marked are read differently and I want to keep the difference straight. The first paragraph is read for its verbs and the tense they sit in, and the note says the verbs are doing the work. The second paragraph is read against the season the book was written, and the note says the weather in the letters that year explains why the drowning is described so flatly. One is about words and one is about the world.

questions.stem: Two paragraphs of the same poem are read differently, and the log asks what kind of claim each is.

options.text: The first is a formal claim about language and the second a historical claim about the moment
Both are formal, since the second paragraph is still made of words and can be counted
options.misconception: treats any written paragraph as a formal object

options.text: Both are historical, since tense choices were made at a particular moment in the past
options.misconception: makes every linguistic choice a historical fact

options.text: Neither is a claim, since a reader may only describe what the two paragraphs plainly contain
options.misconception: restricts reading to plain description

questions.explanation: The first paragraph is read as a formal claim about language and the second as a historical claim about the moment, which is the difference the note is keeping straight. Being made of words, occurring in the past, and plain description each obscure the two kinds of claim.
questions.hint: One reads the words, one reads the world.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a formal reading counts
questions.learningObjective: Explain the limits of a feature count.
questions.stem: An entry explains the limits of a feature count in a formal reading.

answer.exemplar: A feature count has two clear limits and one disputed one. It cannot say what a feature means, since meaning is added by an argument about its work, and it cannot say why a reader should attend to that feature rather than another. The disputed limit is whether a count can distinguish a deliberate effect from an accident, since a repetition may be planned or merely inevitable in a poem of a certain length. A formal reading handles this by describing what the feature does in the arrangement, which is a claim another reader can dispute, rather than by counting alone.

questions.explanation: A count cannot say what a feature means or why it deserves attention, and whether it separates intention from accident is disputed. Describing what a feature does is how the reading turns the tally into a checkable argument.
questions.hint: A count says what, not what it means.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A formal reading asked to connect a device to a subject
questions.learningObjective: Press a formal reading to show a device at work on a subject.
questions.stem: A formal reading is asked to show a device doing work on a subject, and the entry presses.

options.text: The device is established because the poem's critics have agreed on what it does
options.misconception: uses critical agreement as proof that a device works

options.text: The device is established because it appears in every stanza of the printed edition
options.misconception: treats complete distribution as proof of effect

options.text: The device is established once the reading says what changes in the subject because of it
The device is established because the poem's period is known to favour such figures
options.misconception: grounds the effect in a period's taste for figures

questions.explanation: The device is established once the reading states what changes in the subject because of it, since effect is what the reading must demonstrate. Critics' agreement, complete distribution, and a period's taste for figures each substitute a fact for the demonstration.
questions.hint: Say what changes because of it.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Looking for the system beneath a text
questions.learningObjective: Explain what makes a rule set the text's own system.
questions.stem: A reader sets out a system of a text's rules and the log asks what makes it the text's system.

options.text: That the rules hold across the text, including where a reader would not expect them to, and that the text breaks them nowhere
That the rules are numerous, since a system with few rules is only a habit of one book
options.misconception: judges a system by the number of its rules

options.text: That the rules are old, since inherited arrangements are truer systems than new ones
options.misconception: treats age as the sign of a genuine system

options.text: That the writer mentioned them, since a stated method is stronger than an inferred one
options.misconception: requires a writer's statement to make a system real

questions.explanation: A rule set is the text's own system when it holds across the text, including where it is not expected, and where the text departs from it the departure must be the point. Numbers of rules, age, and a stated method each substitute a quality for the fit.
questions.hint: Test it where it is not expected.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A convention mistaken for a statement
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a closing formula actually is.
questions.stem: A closing formula is read as a statement about the world, and the log asks what it is.

options.text: A fixed way of ending, which carries what the form expects rather than what the writer believes
A personal summary, since a writer who chose the ending must be endorsing its statement
options.misconception: treats a chosen ending as an endorsed belief

options.text: A legal pledge, since ending a text in a formula was once a way of binding oneself
options.misconception: reads a literary convention as a literal undertaking

options.text: A decorative flourish, since formulas carry no meaning into the text at all
options.misconception: denies that a formula does any work in the text

questions.explanation: A closing formula carries what the form expects rather than what the writer believes, which is why quoting it as an endorsement misreads it. Endorsement, a literal pledge, and mere decoration each misdescribe a fixed way of ending.
questions.hint: Ask what the form expects of an ending.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a historical reading restores
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a restored context changes in a reading.
questions.stem: A historical reading restores a context and the log asks what the restoration changes.

options.text: It changes what the text's features are taken to be, so the same words now count as usage rather than mystery
It changes the text's value, since a work made in its own moment is always a greater work
options.misconception: judges a text's worth by how well it sits in its period

options.text: It changes the reader's taste, since knowing the period makes a reader prefer its kinds of writing
options.misconception: treats context as a matter of personal preference

options.text: It changes nothing, since a text's meaning was fixed before any history was consulted
options.misconception: insists a fixed meaning is immune to context

questions.explanation: A restored context changes what the text's features are taken to be, so words that looked like mysteries turn out to be usages and the reading is rewritten. Value, taste, and immunity from context each mistake the effect for something else.
questions.hint: The same words, counted differently.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The core claim of a formalist reading
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a formal claim leaves out when it stands alone.
questions.stem: A formal claim is offered as a reading of a whole poem, and the log asks what it leaves out.

options.text: The moment, the audience, and the writer's circumstances, which a second kind of reading must supply
Nothing at all, since the claim was drawn from the poem and the poem contains everything it says
options.misconception: believes a poem contains everything a reading needs

options.text: Only the title, since a poem's arrangement begins after the title page is read
options.misconception: restricts what is left out to one small thing

options.text: The poem's subject, since a formal reading shows how a poem works rather than what it concerns
options.misconception: asserts that arrangement and subject cannot both be discussed

questions.explanation: A formal claim left alone omits the moment, the audience, and the writer's circumstances, which is why it needs a second kind of reading beside it. Totality, a single omission, and the impossibility of joining arrangement to subject each misdescribe the claim's reach.
questions.hint: What still needs another reading?

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A claim about language beside a claim about moment
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a claim about a text's language from one about its first readers.
questions.stem: A claim about a poem's language and a claim about its first readers are set against each other.

options.text: The language claim describes what the poem does with words, the readers claim describes what they were prepared to hear
The language claim is really about readers, since a reader's ear produces the poem's meaning
options.misconception: reduces the poem's language to what its readers made of it

options.text: The readers claim is really about language, since their preparation shows in the poem's vocabulary
options.misconception: reduces a readership to the vocabulary it supplied

options.text: They are the same claim, since a poem's first readers and its words are one historical fact
options.misconception: merges a linguistic claim with a claim about reception

questions.explanation: A language claim describes what the poem does with words, while a readers claim describes what its first audience was prepared to hear, and the two are different objects. Reducing language to reception, reducing reception to vocabulary, and merging them each collapse the distinction.
questions.hint: What the poem does, and what it expected.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a formal reading counts
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate what counting leaves open in a formal reading.
questions.stem: A formal reading is praised for counting and the entry asks what counting leaves open.

options.text: It leaves open the work each feature does, which is where the reading is actually made
It leaves open nothing, since an exact count is the strongest form of a reading
options.misconception: believes precision completes a reading on its own

options.text: It leaves open the author's intention, which is the one thing counting cannot reach
options.misconception: makes intention the only thing a count cannot reach

options.text: It leaves open the reader's agreement, since only the reader's response confirms a count
options.misconception: requires the reader's approval as the test of a count

questions.explanation: Counting leaves open the work each feature does, and that is where the reading is actually made rather than completed. Exactness as completion, intention as the only limit, and the reader's agreement as the test each misplace what the count settles.
questions.hint: The count fixes the facts, not their work.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a historical reading restores
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a historical reading gives back that a formal reading cannot reach.
questions.stem: The log explains what a historical reading gives back that a formal one cannot reach.

answer.exemplar: A historical reading gives back the sense that a text made to its own readers, and that sense includes what the readers expected before they read a word, which formal analysis of arrangement cannot supply because it is not in the arrangement. It also gives back the ordinary, the taken-for-granted, the reasons a particular form was the natural choice that week, so that a reader stops hearing an oddity where there was none. The restoration is of familiarity, and what it makes visible is how much of the text's strangeness was ours alone.

questions.explanation: A historical reading gives back the sense that a text made to its own readers, including their expectations before the first word, which no analysis of arrangement can supply. What it makes visible is how much of a text's strangeness belonged to the reader's own distance.
questions.hint: Restore the familiarity the text assumed.
